comment: Physics multiple choice for the Year 11 modules 10-14. answer is the 0-based index.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which of these materials is attracted to a magnet?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials. Copper, aluminium and zinc are metals but are not magnetic.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which way do magnetic field lines point outside a bar magnet?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Field lines show the direction of the force on a north pole, so outside a magnet they go from the north pole to the south pole.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: On a field diagram, how is a stronger magnetic field shown?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field. Lines spreading apart show the field getting weaker.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: An unmagnetised iron nail is placed near the south pole of a magnet. What happens?
options: It is repelled, because a south pole is induced in it
Nothing, because it is not a magnet
It is attracted, because it becomes positively charged
It is attracted, because a north pole is induced at the end nearest the magnet
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Magnetism is induced in the iron. The near end becomes the opposite pole (north), and opposite poles attract. Charge has nothing to do with it.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Why is steel used to make permanent magnets?
options: It is magnetically hard, so it keeps its magnetism
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Steel is magnetically hard: once magnetised, it keeps its magnetism. Soft iron loses its magnetism easily, which is no good for a permanent magnet.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which statement describes a magnetically soft material?
options: It is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism easily
It keeps its magnetism for a long time
It is only attracted to north poles
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: A soft magnetic material, such as iron, is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism when removed from the field.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: What is the only sure test that a piece of metal is itself a magnet?
options: It is attracted to a magnet
It attracts iron filings only when a current flows
It is repelled by a magnet
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Magnetic materials are attracted to either pole, so attraction proves nothing. Only a magnet can be repelled by another magnet.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: How can two bar magnets be arranged to give a uniform field between them?
options: Two north poles facing each other
Opposite poles facing each other, close together and parallel
The magnets placed side by side, pointing the same way
The magnets at right angles to each other
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Opposite poles (N facing S), close together with parallel faces, give straight, parallel, evenly spaced field lines between them: a uniform field.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which description fits the field lines in a uniform magnetic field?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: A uniform field has the same strength and direction everywhere, so its lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: In the plotting-compass practical, how is a field line drawn?
options: Sprinkle the compass needles on the paper
Mark the needle direction, move the compass along, repeat, then join the dots
Draw a straight line from pole to pole
Tap the compass until it points north
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Mark where the needle points, move the compass to the new dot, repeat, then join the dots into a continuous line.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: In the iron-filings method, why is the card tapped?
options: To help the filings line up along the field lines
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Tapping the card lets the filings move and line up along the field lines, so the pattern shows.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: What shape is the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying a current?
options: Straight lines parallel to the wire
The same as a bar magnet
No field, because the wire is not magnetic
Concentric circles centred on the wire
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The field around a straight wire is a set of concentric circles centred on the wire, getting further apart further away.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A current flows downwards through a card. Seen from above, what is the direction of the magnetic field around the wire?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Right-hand grip rule: thumb along the current (down, away from you), fingers curl clockwise as seen from above.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: What does the field inside a long current-carrying solenoid look like?
options: Straight, parallel lines: a strong, uniform field
Lines that cross in the middle
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Inside a solenoid the field lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced. Outside, the field looks like a bar magnet's.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which is the correct construction of an electromagnet?
options: A coil of wire with a current, wrapped around a soft iron core
A bar magnet with wire wrapped round it
A coil of wire around a steel core with no current
A closed loop of iron with no wire
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: An electromagnet is a coil (solenoid) with a current in it, around a soft iron core. Mark schemes reject a bar magnet and ignore steel.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Why is the core of an electromagnet made of soft iron rather than steel?
options: Soft iron is cheaper to paint
Soft iron keeps its magnetism when the current is off
Steel is not a magnetic material
Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The point of an electromagnet is that it can be switched off. Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current stops; steel would stay magnetised.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which change would make an electromagnet weaker?
options: Using fewer turns on the coil
Adding more turns on the coil
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Fewer turns means a weaker field. More current, more turns and an iron core all make an electromagnet stronger.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Why is there a force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
options: The wire becomes charged and is attracted to the pole
The field of the current interacts with the magnet's field
The wire cuts the field lines and a voltage is induced
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The current makes its own magnetic field, which interacts with the magnet's field to produce a force. Cutting field lines is induction, a different effect.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the second finger represent?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force).

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A current-carrying wire is placed parallel to a magnetic field. What is the force on it?
options: It depends on the direction of the current
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: There is no force when the current is parallel to the field. The force is biggest when the wire is at right angles to the field.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Both the current in a wire and the direction of the magnetic field are reversed. What happens to the force on the wire?
options: It stays in the same direction
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Reversing one of them reverses the force. Reversing both reverses it twice, so the force is in the same direction as before.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which change would NOT increase the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
options: Keeping the wire at right angles to the field
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force but does not change its size. A bigger current or stronger field increases the force.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A proton moves through a magnetic field at right angles to it. What does the force do to the proton?
options: Changes its direction but not its speed
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The force is always at right angles to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed. The proton moves in a curve.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: An electron moves to the right through a magnetic field. Which way should the second finger point in the left-hand rule?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The second finger shows conventional current. An electron is negative, so the current is opposite to its motion: to the left.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Two parallel wires both carry current in the same direction. What happens?
options: They repel because they have the same charge
They attract, because each wire is a current in the other's magnetic field
Nothing, because currents do not affect each other
They attract because they have opposite charges
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Each wire has a magnetic field, so each is a current in the other's field and feels a force towards the other. It is not an electrostatic effect.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Why does the coil of a d.c. motor turn?
options: The coil's north pole is attracted to the magnet's south pole
The coil cuts field lines and a voltage is induced
The magnet heats one side of the coil
The forces on opposite sides of the coil are in opposite directions
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The current goes one way along one side and back along the other, so the forces are in opposite directions and the coil turns. Mark schemes ignore attraction and repulsion answers.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: What does the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor do?
options: Reverses the current in the coil every half turn
Changes a.c. into a higher voltage
Stops the coil from turning too fast
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: It reverses the current every half turn, so the forces keep turning the coil in the same direction instead of rocking back.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Why does the cone of a loudspeaker vibrate?
options: The coil cuts field lines and induces a voltage
The alternating current makes the force on the coil keep changing direction
The magnet vibrates on its own
The cone is charged and repelled by the magnet
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The a.c. keeps reversing, so the force from the interacting fields keeps reversing. The coil and cone are pushed back and forth: they vibrate and make sound.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A wire is held still between the poles of a strong magnet and connected to a sensitive ammeter. What does the ammeter read?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: A voltage is induced only when the wire cuts field lines or the field changes. A still wire in a steady field cuts no lines, so there is no induced current.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which change would increase the voltage induced when a wire is moved through a magnetic field?
options: Moving the wire along the field lines
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Faster movement, a stronger magnet or a coil with more turns all increase the induced voltage. Moving along the field lines cuts none, so gives zero.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A wire moved between two poles gives an induced current of 2.8 mA. The poles are reversed and the movement repeated in the same way. What is the reading?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Reversing the field reverses the induced current. It is the same size in the opposite direction: −2.8 mA.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A generator has a coil rotating in a magnetic field. Why is its output alternating?
options: The magnet keeps switching on and off
Each side of the coil moves up and then down through the field, so the induced voltage reverses
The coil is connected to the mains
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Each side of the coil cuts the field one way, then the other way, every turn, so the induced voltage keeps reversing: a.c.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which would NOT increase the voltage from a generator?
options: Using a coil with fewer turns
Using a coil with more turns
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Fewer turns means a smaller induced voltage. Faster rotation, a stronger magnet and more turns all increase it.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: What are the main parts of a transformer?
options: One coil wound around a steel bar magnet
A coil and a split-ring commutator
A primary coil and a secondary coil wound on a soft iron core
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: A transformer is two coils, the primary and the secondary, on the same soft iron core. The core carries the changing field to the secondary.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Why will a transformer not work on a constant d.c. supply?
options: A constant current gives a constant field, and induction needs a changing field
d.c. only flows in the secondary coil
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Induction needs a changing magnetic field. Constant d.c. makes a constant field in the core, so no voltage is induced in the secondary.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 1000 turns on the secondary. The input voltage is 12 V. What is the output voltage?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Vp ÷ Vs = np ÷ ns, so 12 ÷ Vs = 200 ÷ 1000. Vs = 12 × 1000 ÷ 200 = 60 V. It is a step-up transformer.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: A 100% efficient transformer steps 230 V down to 11.5 V. The primary current is 0.10 A. What is the secondary current?
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is, so 230 × 0.10 = 11.5 × Is. Is = 23 ÷ 11.5 = 2.0 A. The voltage went down 20 times, so the current went up 20 times.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Why is electricity transmitted in the National Grid at a very high voltage?
options: High voltage makes the electricity travel faster
The current is lower, so there is less heating and less energy wasted in the cables
High voltage is safer for people near the cables
Transformers only work at high voltage
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: For the same power (P = I × V), a higher voltage means a lower current. A lower current means less heating in the cables, so less energy is wasted.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: Which statement correctly describes alternating current (a.c.)?
options: It flows in one direction only
It is supplied by a cell or battery
It is always smaller than d.c.
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: a.c. keeps changing direction, again and again. d.c. from a cell or battery flows in one direction only. Mains electricity is a.c.

10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.q: The live wire in a kettle touches its metal case, which is earthed. What happens?
options: A large current flows to earth and the fuse melts, breaking the circuit
The case becomes live and stays live
The earth wire melts instead of the fuse
The current falls to zero straight away, with no fuse needed
10-magnetism-and-electromagnetism.explain: The earth wire has a low resistance, so a large current flows through it to earth. This is more than the fuse rating, so the fuse melts and cuts off the supply.

11-momentum.q: Which is the correct equation for momentum?
11-momentum.explain: p = m × v, which you must learn. Mass × acceleration is force.

11-momentum.q: What is the unit of momentum?
11-momentum.explain: From p = m × v: kilograms × metres per second = kg m/s. kg m/s² is the newton.

11-momentum.q: A 0.41 kg bird flies at 13 m/s. What is its momentum?
11-momentum.explain: p = 0.41 × 13 = 5.33 kg m/s (2023 Edexcel 2P Q4). 31.7 comes from dividing 13 by 0.41.

11-momentum.q: Why is momentum a vector quantity?
options: Because it is measured in kg m/s
Because it can never be zero
11-momentum.explain: Mass is a scalar, but velocity has size and direction, so mass × velocity has a direction too.

11-momentum.q: A 2 kg trolley moves right at 3 m/s. Another 2 kg trolley moves left at 3 m/s. Taking right as positive, what is their total momentum?
11-momentum.explain: +6 + (−6) = 0. Momenta in opposite directions cancel. 12 comes from ignoring direction.

11-momentum.q: Which statement is the principle of conservation of momentum?
options: Momentum is always lost in a collision
The momentum of each object stays the same in a collision
Total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after, if no external forces act
Momentum is converted into kinetic energy in a collision
11-momentum.explain: It is the total that is conserved, not each object's momentum. One object gains what the other loses.

11-momentum.q: Two objects are at rest and then push apart. What is their total momentum afterwards?
options: Equal to the momentum of the heavier object
Equal to the momentum of the faster object
Twice the momentum of either object
11-momentum.explain: It was zero before, so it is zero after. The two momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction.

11-momentum.q: A rifle fires a bullet. Why does the rifle move back much more slowly than the bullet moves forward?
options: The rifle has less momentum than the bullet
Some of the momentum is lost as sound
The rifle's momentum is in the same direction as the bullet's
The rifle has the same size of momentum but a much larger mass
11-momentum.explain: The momenta are equal and opposite. Same momentum with a bigger mass means a smaller velocity.

11-momentum.q: A 1.9 kg object moves off at 3.7 m/s after pushing apart from a 2.9 kg object at rest. What is the velocity of the 2.9 kg object?
11-momentum.explain: 0 = 1.9 × 3.7 + 2.9v, so v = −7.03 ÷ 2.9 = −2.4 m/s (2022 Edexcel 2P Q2). The minus sign means the opposite direction.

11-momentum.q: A 0.60 kg hawk at 12 m/s catches a 0.30 kg pigeon at 3.0 m/s flying the same way. What is their velocity together?
11-momentum.explain: Total momentum = 7.2 + 0.9 = 8.1 kg m/s. Divide by the total mass 0.90 kg: 9.0 m/s. 13.5 comes from dividing by 0.60 kg only; 8.1 is the momentum, not the velocity.

11-momentum.q: Two objects collide and stick together. Which mass do you use to find their velocity afterwards?
options: The mass of the heavier object
The mass of the faster object
The total mass of both objects
The difference between the two masses
11-momentum.explain: After joining they move as one object, so velocity = total momentum ÷ total mass.

11-momentum.q: Two objects collide and stick together. The final velocity must be…
options: equal to the faster starting velocity
11-momentum.explain: The fast one slows down and the slow one speeds up, so the shared velocity is between them. A quick check on any answer.

11-momentum.q: Which equation links force, change in momentum and time?
11-momentum.explain: Force = change in momentum ÷ time taken. It is on the formula sheet.

11-momentum.q: A driver's momentum of 936 kg m/s falls to zero in 0.29 s. What is the average force on the driver?
11-momentum.explain: F = 936 ÷ 0.29 = 3228 N, about 3200 N (2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q1(b)). 271 N comes from multiplying by 0.29 instead of dividing.

11-momentum.q: A 1200 kg car speeds up from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 6.0 s. What is the resultant force?
11-momentum.explain: Change in momentum = 30 000 − 12 000 = 18 000 kg m/s. 18 000 ÷ 6.0 = 3000 N. 5000 N uses only the final momentum.

11-momentum.q: Force is equal to…
options: the total momentum of an object
the rate of change of momentum
11-momentum.explain: F = change in momentum ÷ time, which is the rate of change of momentum. Momentum ÷ mass is velocity.

11-momentum.q: A 0.20 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m/s and bounces back at 6.0 m/s. What is the size of its change in momentum?
11-momentum.explain: +1.6 to −1.2: the change is −1.2 − 1.6 = −2.8, size 2.8 kg m/s. 0.4 ignores the change of direction.

11-momentum.q: A ball hits a wall and bounces back at the same speed. Compared with a ball that stops dead, the change in momentum is…
11-momentum.explain: From +p to −p is a change of 2p, compared with p for stopping. So the force is twice as big for the same contact time.

11-momentum.q: How does an airbag reduce the force on a driver in a crash?
options: It reduces the driver's change in momentum
It increases the time taken for the driver to stop
11-momentum.explain: The change in momentum is fixed (speed to zero). A longer time means a smaller rate of change of momentum, so a smaller force.

11-momentum.q: In a crash, what is the same whether or not the car has a crumple zone?
options: The rate of change of momentum
11-momentum.explain: The passengers go from the same speed to zero either way. The crumple zone changes the time, and so the rate of change of momentum and the force.

11-momentum.q: Which answer would score the marks for how a crumple zone works?
options: It absorbs the momentum of the crash
It increases the time to stop, so the rate of change of momentum and the force are smaller
It makes the car lighter so it has less momentum
It cushions the impact so it is softer
11-momentum.explain: The mark scheme wants time up, rate of change of momentum down, force down. 'Absorbs' and 'cushions' are too vague.

11-momentum.q: An egg dropped on a carpet does not break, but one dropped on a hard floor does. Why?
options: The carpet reduces the egg's momentum before it lands
The carpet increases the egg's change in momentum
The carpet pushes up with a bigger force
The carpet increases the impact time, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller
11-momentum.explain: 2022 Edexcel 2P Q2(c): the scheme credited the carpet increasing the impact time and reducing the rate of change of momentum.

11-momentum.q: How does a seat belt reduce injury, in momentum terms?
options: It stretches, increasing the time for the passenger to stop
It makes the passenger stop in a shorter time
It reduces the car's speed before the crash
11-momentum.explain: The belt stretches slightly, so the passenger stops over a longer time, so the force on them is smaller.

11-momentum.q: Why does a cycle helmet have a foam lining?
options: The foam makes the head lighter, so it has less momentum
The foam reduces the head's change in momentum
The foam compresses, increasing the time for the head to stop
The foam increases the force on the head so it stops quickly
11-momentum.explain: Compressing foam lengthens the stopping time, so the force on the skull is smaller.

11-momentum.q: A cricketer pulls her hands back as she catches a ball. This…
options: increases the time to stop the ball, reducing the force on her hands
reduces the ball's momentum before she catches it
reduces the change in momentum of the ball
increases the rate of change of momentum
11-momentum.explain: The same argument as a crumple zone: longer time, smaller rate of change of momentum, smaller force.

11-momentum.q: A car stops in 0.12 s in a crash. With a crumple zone it would stop in 0.30 s. The force with the crumple zone is…
11-momentum.explain: Same change in momentum, 2.5 times the time, so 2.5 times less force.

11-momentum.q: A 58 g tennis ball leaves a racket at 50 m/s from rest. What is its change in momentum?
11-momentum.explain: 58 g = 0.058 kg. 0.058 × 50 = 2.9 kg m/s. 2900 comes from forgetting to convert grams to kilograms.

11-momentum.q: A trolley of 2.0 kg at 3.0 m/s right hits a 1.0 kg trolley at 2.0 m/s left. They stick. What is their velocity?
11-momentum.explain: Total momentum = 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 kg m/s; 4.0 ÷ 3.0 = 1.3 m/s right. 2.7 m/s comes from adding 6.0 and 2.0.

11-momentum.q: Two skaters at rest push apart. A (60 kg) moves at 2.0 m/s; B moves the other way at 3.0 m/s. What is B's mass?
11-momentum.explain: 60 × 2.0 = 120 kg m/s = m × 3.0, so m = 40 kg. B moves faster, so B must be lighter. 90 kg has the ratio upside down.

11-momentum.q: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
11-momentum.explain: Bullet momentum = 4.0 kg m/s. The rifle has the same size of momentum backwards: 4.0 ÷ 4.0 = 1.0 m/s.

11-momentum.q: When is momentum NOT conserved for two colliding objects?
options: When a large external force such as friction acts on them
When one of them starts at rest
11-momentum.explain: Conservation holds in the absence of external forces. Sticking, bouncing or starting at rest do not break it.

11-momentum.q: Why is momentum conserved when two objects collide?
options: They exert equal and opposite forces on each other for the same time
The heavier object always keeps its momentum
The forces between them are always zero
11-momentum.explain: By Newton's third law the forces are equal and opposite, and act for the same time, so the momentum changes are equal and opposite.

11-momentum.q: Which has the greatest momentum?
11-momentum.explain: Lorry: 6000 kg m/s. Runner: 300. Bullet: 4. Ball: 4.8. You have to multiply mass by velocity; speed alone does not decide it.

11-momentum.q: A 0.16 kg ball at 2.5 m/s hits an identical ball at rest and carries on at 0.50 m/s. What is the second ball's velocity?
11-momentum.explain: 0.40 = 0.08 + 0.16v, so v = 0.32 ÷ 0.16 = 2.0 m/s. 0.32 is the momentum, not the velocity.

11-momentum.q: In a momentum calculation, an answer comes out as −3.0 m/s. What does the minus sign mean?
options: The object has less momentum than before
The object moves in the direction you chose as negative
11-momentum.explain: Momentum and velocity are vectors. A negative answer is a direction, opposite to the one you chose as positive.

11-momentum.q: A 65 kg driver moves at 15 m/s. An airbag stops him in 0.25 s. What is the average force?
11-momentum.explain: Momentum = 65 × 15 = 975 kg m/s. F = 975 ÷ 0.25 = 3900 N. 244 N comes from multiplying by 0.25.

11-momentum.q: F = (mv − mu) ÷ t is the same as which other equation?
11-momentum.explain: (mv − mu) ÷ t = m × (v − u) ÷ t, and (v − u) ÷ t is the acceleration.

11-momentum.q: A 1500 kg car at 20 m/s has momentum…
11-momentum.explain: 1500 × 20 = 30 000 kg m/s. 75 comes from dividing mass by velocity.

11-momentum.q: A stationary object explodes into two pieces. Which statement is correct?
options: Both pieces move in the same direction
The pieces have equal and opposite momentum
The pieces always have equal speeds
11-momentum.explain: Total momentum stays zero, so the momenta are equal and opposite. The speeds are equal only if the masses are equal; the lighter piece is faster.

11-momentum.q: Which is true about a safety feature in a crash?
options: It reduces the change in momentum of the passenger
It increases the force on the passenger
It reduces the rate of change of momentum of the passenger
11-momentum.explain: The change in momentum is fixed; the feature increases the time, so the rate of change of momentum (the force) is smaller.

12-light-and-refraction.q: What type of wave is light?
options: A wave that needs a medium
A wave whose vibrations are parallel to its direction of travel
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Light is a transverse wave: its vibrations are at right angles to its direction of travel. Sound is the longitudinal one.

12-light-and-refraction.q: From which line are the angles of incidence, reflection and refraction measured?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Every angle in this topic is measured from the normal, a line at 90° to the surface where the ray meets it.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which piece of apparatus is used to measure the angles in a reflection or refraction practical?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: A protractor measures angles. This was a 1-mark question on 2022 Jan 1P and 2023 2P.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which statement is the law of reflection?
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of refraction
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The angle of reflection is always 90°
The angle of incidence plus the angle of reflection equals 90°
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at 20° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal: 90 − 20 = 70°. The angle of reflection equals it, 70°.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: The rays sit either side of the normal, each at 35° to it, so the angle between them is 35 + 35 = 70°.

12-light-and-refraction.q: What causes refraction?
options: A change in the speed of the wave as it enters a new material
A change in the frequency of the wave
The wave bouncing off the boundary
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Refraction is a change in direction caused by a change of speed when a wave crosses into a different material. The frequency does not change.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray of light passes from air into glass at an angle. What happens?
options: It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It speeds up and bends towards the normal
It slows down and bends towards the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Glass is optically denser than air, so light slows down and bends towards the normal.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray of light passes from water out into air at an angle. Which way does it bend?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Light speeds up going from water into air, so it bends away from the normal. The angle in air is bigger.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray of light hits a glass block along the normal. What happens as it enters the glass?
options: It slows down but does not change direction
It does not slow down or change direction
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Along the normal (i = 0°) the light still slows down, but it does not change direction.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray passes into and out of a rectangular glass block through two parallel sides. How does the emerging ray compare with the incident ray?
options: It is at right angles to the incident ray
It is parallel to the incident ray, shifted sideways
It travels back the way it came
It is bent towards the base of the block
12-light-and-refraction.explain: The two bends cancel because the faces are parallel, so the ray leaves parallel to its original direction, displaced sideways.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which is the correct equation for refractive index?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: n = sin i ÷ sin r, where i is the angle in air and r the angle in the material. Dividing the angles themselves is rejected.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A student measures i = 44° and r = 28° for a glass prism. What is the refractive index?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: n = sin 44° ÷ sin 28° = 0.695 ÷ 0.469 = 1.48, which is 1.5 to 2 s.f. 44 ÷ 28 = 1.57 is the rejected answer.

12-light-and-refraction.q: What is the unit of refractive index?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Refractive index is one sine divided by another, so it has no unit.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray enters glass of refractive index 1.5 with an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of refraction?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: sin r = sin 40° ÷ 1.5 = 0.643 ÷ 1.5 = 0.429, so r = 25°. It is smaller than 40°, as it must be entering glass.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A diagram shows a refracted ray inside a prism making 54° with the surface. What is the angle of refraction?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Angles are measured from the normal: 90 − 54 = 36°. This was 2022 Jan 1P Q10(a)(i).

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which is a typical refractive index for glass?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Glass is about 1.5 and water 1.33. Refractive index is always more than 1 for these materials.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Why is the refractive index of glass always greater than 1?
options: Light bends towards the normal in glass, so sin i is bigger than sin r
Glass reflects most of the light
The angle of refraction is bigger than the angle of incidence
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Light slows and bends towards the normal, so r is smaller than i and sin i ÷ sin r is more than 1.

12-light-and-refraction.q: In the glass block practical, why should the crosses marking the emerging ray be placed far apart?
options: So the line drawn through them is more accurate
So the block does not move
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Crosses far apart give a more accurate direction for the ray, so the angles are measured more accurately.

12-light-and-refraction.q: A student plots sin i on the y-axis against sin r on the x-axis for a glass block. What does the gradient give?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: sin i = n × sin r, so a graph of sin i against sin r is a straight line through the origin with gradient n.

12-light-and-refraction.q: In a semi-circular block experiment, why is the ray aimed at the centre of the flat face through the curved side?
options: So it enters along a normal and does not bend at the curved side
So it is totally internally reflected at the curved side
So it speeds up as it enters
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Aimed at the centre, the ray travels along a radius, which is normal to the curved surface, so it does not bend going in. All the bending happens at the flat face.

12-light-and-refraction.q: White light passes through a prism. Which colour is refracted the most?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Violet is bent the most and red the least, so the colours spread out.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Red light has a longer wavelength than violet and is refracted less by glass. What can you deduce?
options: Refractive index is the same for all colours
Refractive index increases as wavelength increases
Red light travels more slowly in glass
Refractive index decreases as wavelength increases
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Red refracts less, so it has a lower refractive index. Red has the longer wavelength, so refractive index decreases as wavelength increases (2022 Jan 1P Q10(b)).

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which is the correct definition of the critical angle?
options: The angle of refraction when the angle of incidence is 90°
The angle of incidence in the denser material for which the angle of refraction is 90°
The largest angle a mirror can reflect
The angle at which light stops travelling
12-light-and-refraction.explain: The critical angle is the angle of incidence, inside the denser material, that gives an angle of refraction of 90°.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which pair of conditions is needed for total internal reflection?
options: Light going from less dense to more dense; angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
Light going from more dense to less dense; angle of incidence less than the critical angle
Light going from more dense to less dense; angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
Any material; angle of incidence of exactly 90°
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Both are needed: light going from the denser to the less dense material, and an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Why can light going from air into water never be totally internally reflected?
options: It is going into the denser material, so it bends towards the normal
The critical angle of water is 90°
Light does not slow down in water
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Total internal reflection needs light going from denser to less dense. Going into water, the ray bends towards the normal and can always get in.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which is the correct equation linking critical angle and refractive index?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: sin c = 1 ÷ n. Use sin⁻¹ to find c.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Glass has a refractive index of 1.50. What is its critical angle?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: sin c = 1 ÷ 1.50 = 0.667, so c = sin⁻¹ 0.667 = 41.8°, which is 42°. 0.67 is the sine, not the angle.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Water has a refractive index of 1.33. What is its critical angle?
A block has a critical angle of 43°. What is its refractive index?
Material X has a higher refractive index than material Y. How do their critical angles compare?
options: X has a larger critical angle
X has a smaller critical angle
12-light-and-refraction.explain: sin c = 1 ÷ n, so a bigger n gives a smaller sin c and a smaller critical angle.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Light inside glass (critical angle 42°) meets a glass/air boundary at an angle of incidence of 30°. What happens?
options: Most of it refracts out into the air, bending away from the normal
It refracts out, bending towards the normal
12-light-and-refraction.explain: 30° is less than the critical angle, so the light refracts out, bending away from the normal. A weak reflected ray is also present.

12-light-and-refraction.q: At the critical angle, where does the refracted ray go?
options: Along the boundary, at 90° to the normal
Straight back along the incident ray
12-light-and-refraction.explain: At the critical angle the angle of refraction is 90°, so the refracted ray skims along the boundary.

12-light-and-refraction.q: As the angle of incidence inside a semi-circular block is increased towards the critical angle, what happens to the reflected ray?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: The refracted ray gets dimmer and the reflected ray gets brighter. Above the critical angle all the light is reflected.

12-light-and-refraction.q: How does light travel along an optical fibre?
options: By refraction at every point along the fibre
By total internal reflection at the sides of the fibre
By bouncing off a mirror coating
12-light-and-refraction.explain: The light meets the sides at more than the critical angle, going from dense glass to a less dense material, so it is totally internally reflected many times.

12-light-and-refraction.q: On 2023 Jan 1P Q6, which reason was credited for total internal reflection in an optical fibre?
options: The light travels faster in the core
The angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle
12-light-and-refraction.explain: The scheme gave marks for total internal reflection, the core having a higher refractive index, and the angle of incidence being greater than the critical angle.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Which statement about waves in optical fibre communication is correct?
options: Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter
Waves transfer energy, information and matter
Waves transfer matter but not energy
Waves transfer energy without transferring information
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter. This was 2023 Jan 1P Q6(a).

12-light-and-refraction.q: A ray enters a 45°–45°–90° glass prism along the normal to a short face and hits the long face at 45°. The critical angle is 42°. What happens?
options: It refracts out of the long face
It is totally internally reflected and turned through 90°
It passes straight through without changing direction
12-light-and-refraction.explain: 45° is greater than 42°, and the light is going from glass to air, so it is totally internally reflected and turned through 90°, as in a periscope.

12-light-and-refraction.q: What type of wave is sound?
options: Longitudinal, and can be reflected and refracted
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Sound is longitudinal and, like all waves, can be reflected (an echo) and refracted.

12-light-and-refraction.q: Sound travels faster in water than in air. Which way does sound bend when it passes from air into water at an angle?
12-light-and-refraction.explain: Sound speeds up going into water, so it bends away from the normal: the opposite way to light.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which colour of star has the hottest surface?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A star's colour depends on its surface temperature. Blue stars are the hottest and red stars are the coolest.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Betelgeuse is red. Rigel is blue. What can you conclude?
options: Betelgeuse is closer to the Earth
Rigel has a hotter surface than Betelgeuse
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Colour tells you surface temperature. Blue means a hotter surface than red. Colour alone does not tell you distance, age or mass.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which list puts star colours in order of increasing surface temperature?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Coolest to hottest: red, orange, yellow, white, blue.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: A student says a star is the hottest in a table because it has the largest mass. How would the mark scheme treat this reason?
options: It is ignored: the reason must link colour to surface temperature
It is accepted if the star is also the biggest
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: In 2023 the scheme said to ignore links between mass and temperature. The mark is for saying colour depends on surface temperature.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What is a nebula?
options: A dying star that has exploded
A group of billions of stars
A small, dense star with no fusion
A cloud of gas and dust in space
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A nebula is a cloud of gas (mostly hydrogen) and dust. Stars form when part of it collapses under gravity. A galaxy is a group of billions of stars.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What makes a nebula collapse to form a star?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Gravity pulls the gas and dust together. Fusion only starts later, once the core is hot enough.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: As a nebula collapses to form a star, what happens to the gravitational potential energy store of the gas?
options: It is transferred to the nuclear store
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The gas falls inwards, so its gravitational potential store decreases. The energy goes to the thermal store, which is why the protostar heats up.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What is the energy source of a main sequence star?
options: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
Burning of hydrogen gas with oxygen
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Fusion is the energy source for stars. Fission is splitting large nuclei; burning is a chemical reaction; alpha decay is radioactivity.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: When does a star leave the main sequence?
options: When it becomes a white dwarf
When its outer layers cool down
When the hydrogen in its core runs out
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A main sequence star fuses hydrogen in its core. When that hydrogen runs out, it expands into a red giant or red supergiant.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which is the correct life cycle for a star of similar mass to the Sun?
options: nebula → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova
nebula → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf
nebula → red giant → main sequence → white dwarf
nebula → main sequence → white dwarf → red giant
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Sun-like stars go nebula, (protostar), main sequence, red giant, white dwarf. Supergiants and supernovae are for much more massive stars.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which property of a star decides whether it becomes a red giant or a red supergiant?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Mass decides the path. In 2024 the mark scheme said to ignore size and weight.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What is left behind when a red giant sheds its outer layers?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A red giant throws off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, and its hot, dense core remains as a white dwarf. Neutron stars and black holes come from supernovae.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which statement correctly compares a red giant with a white dwarf?
options: The red giant is larger and has a lower surface temperature
The red giant is smaller and hotter
The white dwarf is brighter and larger
Both have fusion in their cores
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A red giant is huge with a cool (red) surface; a white dwarf is tiny and hot. Fusion still happens in a red giant but not in a white dwarf.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Why does a white dwarf slowly fade?
options: It is moving away from the Earth
It is losing mass in a supernova
No fusion takes place in it, so it cools
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A white dwarf has no fusion. It is just a hot leftover core that gradually cools and fades.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which of these is much denser than a red giant?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A white dwarf packs about a Sun's worth of mass into something about the size of the Earth, so it is extremely dense. A red giant is spread out and has low density.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What is a planetary nebula?
options: A cloud of gas from which planets form
A planet that has been destroyed by its star
A disc of rocks around a young star
The shell of gas thrown off by a red giant
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets. It is the outer layers of a red giant, leaving a white dwarf in the middle.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: A star much more massive than the Sun leaves the main sequence. What does it become?
options: A red giant, then a white dwarf
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: High-mass stars become red supergiants, then explode as supernovae.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What happens to a red supergiant at the end of its life?
options: It shrinks quietly into a white dwarf
It becomes a main sequence star again
It turns into a nebula and forms planets
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A red supergiant collapses and explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: After a supernova, what can be left behind?
options: A red giant or a white dwarf
A neutron star or a black hole
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The remnant of a supernova is a neutron star, or for the most massive stars, a black hole.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Rigel has 21 solar masses. Sirius has 2 solar masses. Which statement is correct?
options: Rigel will become a red giant and Sirius a supernova
Rigel will become a supernova and Sirius a white dwarf
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Rigel is a high-mass star: red supergiant, supernova, neutron star. Sirius is low mass, like the Sun: red giant, white dwarf.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What is absolute magnitude?
options: How bright a star looks from Earth
The mass of a star compared with the Sun
The surface temperature of a star
The brightness of a star at a standard distance
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Absolute magnitude is brightness at a standard distance. Two marks in 2024: brightness (1), standard distance (1).

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Why is absolute magnitude used instead of how bright stars look from Earth?
options: It removes the effect of different distances
It measures the star's temperature more accurately
It shows how old the star is
It includes the mass of the star
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: How bright a star looks depends on how far away it is. Comparing at the same standard distance is a fair comparison of the stars themselves.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Star P has an absolute magnitude of −3. Star Q has an absolute magnitude of +6. Which is correct?
options: Q gives out more light because its number is bigger
They give out the same light
P gives out more light because a lower number means brighter
You cannot tell without their distances
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The magnitude scale runs backwards: lower (more negative) means brighter. Absolute magnitude already accounts for distance.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: On an HR diagram, what is plotted on the vertical axis?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The vertical axis is absolute magnitude (brightness), with the brightest stars at the top. Colour or temperature goes along the horizontal axis.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: On an HR diagram, where are the hottest stars?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The temperature axis runs 'backwards': hot blue stars on the left, cool red stars on the right.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: On an HR diagram, where are white dwarfs found?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: White dwarfs are hot (left) but dim (bottom), because they are tiny.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: On an HR diagram, where are red giants found?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Red giants are cool (right) but very bright (top), because they are enormous.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which describes the main sequence on an HR diagram?
options: A diagonal band from top left to bottom right
A horizontal line across the middle
A vertical line on the right-hand side
A small group at the bottom left
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The main sequence runs from hot, bright stars at the top left to cool, dim stars at the bottom right. The Sun is in the middle of it.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: According to the Big Bang theory, how have the size and temperature of the universe changed?
options: It has been expanding and cooling
It has been expanding and heating up
It has been shrinking and cooling
Its size and temperature have stayed the same
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The universe began extremely hot and dense at a single point. Since then it has expanded and cooled. One mark for each idea in 2022.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Which two pieces of evidence support the Big Bang theory?
options: Fusion in stars and the colours of stars
Red-shift of galaxies and the CMB radiation
The orbits of planets and comets
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The spec names red-shift and cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation as the evidence.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: A galaxy is moving away from the Earth. What happens to the light we receive from it?
options: Its wavelength decreases and frequency increases
It travels more slowly than normal light
Its wavelength increases and frequency decreases
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The source moves away between wavefronts, so they arrive further apart: longer wavelength, lower frequency. The speed of light is unchanged. The light is shifted towards the red end, not turned red.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Light from a galaxy moving towards the Earth is observed. What is this called?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: A source moving towards us gives a shorter wavelength and higher frequency: a shift towards the blue end.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: In the equation Δλ ÷ λ₀ = v ÷ c, what is λ₀?
options: The reference wavelength, as emitted by the source
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: λ₀ is the reference wavelength. Using the observed wavelength instead cost all but 1 mark in 2023.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Light with a reference wavelength of 600 nm arrives with a wavelength of 612 nm. Speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the speed of the galaxy?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Δλ = 12 nm. v = (12 ÷ 600) × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 6.0 × 10⁶ m/s. Dividing by 612 (the observed wavelength) gives 5.9 × 10⁶, the classic error.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: A galaxy moves away at 1.5 × 10⁷ m/s. Light is emitted at 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m. Speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the change in wavelength?
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Δλ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ × (1.5 × 10⁷ ÷ 3.0 × 10⁸) = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ × 0.05 = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ m. 6.3 × 10⁻⁷ m is the received wavelength, not the change.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What do astronomers observe about the red-shift of galaxies at different distances?
options: All galaxies have the same red-shift
The further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Greater red-shift for more distant galaxies means the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Galaxy B has twice the red-shift of galaxy A. What does this tell you?
options: B is twice as hot as A
B is moving away twice as fast as A
B is twice as massive as A
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Red-shift is proportional to speed: twice the red-shift, twice the speed of recession. This link was the first mark in 2023 2P Q7(b)(iii).

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Why is the red-shift of galaxies evidence that the universe is expanding?
options: Red light has the longest wavelength
Galaxies are getting redder as they age
The further away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away, so galaxies are moving apart
Stars at the edge of the universe are all red giants
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: Further galaxies move away faster, so galaxies are moving apart: the universe is expanding. Run backwards, it started at a single point.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: What is the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation?
options: Microwaves from stars in the Milky Way
Microwave radiation from all directions, left over from the early hot universe
Radiation given out by black holes
Microwaves reflected from the Earth's atmosphere
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The CMB comes from every direction and is left over from the hot early universe. That it is the same in all directions suggests all parts of the universe were once in contact.

13-stars-and-the-universe.q: Why is the CMB radiation now in the microwave region?
options: Microwaves travel faster than other radiation
Stars have been giving out more microwaves over time
The expansion of the universe has stretched its wavelength
13-stars-and-the-universe.explain: The radiation was emitted when the universe was very hot, at short wavelengths. As the universe expanded, its wavelength increased into the microwave region.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: In which direction is thermal energy always transferred between two objects?
options: From the hotter object to the colder object
From the colder object to the hotter object
From the larger object to the smaller object
From the denser object to the less dense object
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Energy flows from hot to cold until both reach the same temperature. Cold does not flow anywhere.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: By which mechanism is energy mainly transferred through a solid metal rod?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Solids transfer energy by conduction. Convection needs a fluid that can flow.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why are metals better thermal conductors than other solids?
options: They contain free electrons that carry energy through the metal
Their particles can flow like a liquid
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Metals have free (delocalised) electrons that move through the metal and carry energy quickly, on top of the vibrating particles.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Which mechanism of energy transfer can take place through a vacuum?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Infrared radiation is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium. Conduction and convection both need particles.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: When air is heated, why does it rise?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: The particles move faster and spread further apart, so the air expands and becomes less dense. The particles themselves do not get bigger.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Which type of surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Dark matt surfaces are the best absorbers (and emitters). Light shiny surfaces are the worst.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Which type of surface is the poorest emitter of infrared radiation?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Light shiny surfaces are the poorest emitters and the best reflectors.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: In which states of matter can convection take place?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Convection needs the material to flow, so it only happens in fluids: liquids and gases. Particles in a solid are fixed in place.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Which is the best description of conduction in a non-metal solid?
options: Warm parts of the solid rise and cool parts sink
Particles vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles
Infrared waves pass through the solid
Free electrons carry energy through the solid
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: In a non-metal there are no free electrons, so energy passes only by vibrating particles passing energy to their neighbours.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: What is the main purpose of the vacuum in a vacuum flask?
options: To reflect infrared back into the flask
To stop evaporation from the top
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: A vacuum has no particles, so conduction and convection cannot happen across it. Radiation can still cross a vacuum; the silvering deals with that.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why are the walls of a vacuum flask silvered?
options: To reduce energy transfer by radiation
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Shiny surfaces are poor emitters and good reflectors of infrared, so they reduce transfer by radiation.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why is the heating element of a kettle placed at the bottom?
options: So that convection currents carry heated water upwards through all the water
So that the element is kept away from the lid
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Heated water at the bottom becomes less dense and rises; cooler, denser water sinks to be heated. A convection current heats all the water.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why is the freezer compartment usually at the top of a fridge?
options: Cold air rises to the top
Cooled air becomes denser and sinks, setting up a convection current
Cold is conducted downwards through the shelves
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Air cooled at the top is denser and sinks; warmer air rises to be cooled, so the whole fridge is cooled by convection.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Loft insulation such as mineral wool reduces energy transfer mainly because it:
options: reflects infrared back into the house
traps air, which is a poor conductor and cannot form convection currents
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Trapped air is a poor conductor, and because it cannot move, convection currents cannot form.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why is an empty wall cavity a poorer insulator than one filled with foam?
options: Air in an empty cavity can circulate in convection currents
Foam is a good emitter of infrared
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: In an empty cavity the air can move and carry energy by convection. Foam traps the air in small pockets so it cannot circulate.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: How does energy from the Sun reach the Earth?
options: By infrared and other electromagnetic radiation
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Space is a vacuum with no particles, so only radiation can cross it.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Two identical cans, one matt black and one shiny silver, are filled with the same volume of hot water at the same temperature. What happens?
options: Both cool at the same rate
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Matt black is a better emitter of infrared, so the black can loses energy faster and cools faster.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Two identical bottles of cold water, one black and one silver, are placed the same distance from an infrared heater. What happens?
options: The silver bottle warms faster because it reflects infrared
Both warm at the same rate
Neither warms, because infrared needs a medium
The black bottle warms faster because it is a better absorber
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Black absorbs more infrared, so more energy is transferred to it in the same time. Both warm up; black is always ahead.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: White snow in direct sunlight takes a long time to melt. Why?
options: White snow is a poor absorber and good reflector of infrared
White snow is a good conductor
White snow is a good absorber of infrared
Convection currents carry energy into the snow
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: White surfaces reflect most infrared and absorb little, so the snow gains energy slowly.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Snow melts faster on a metal drain cover than on the ground around it. Which is the best explanation?
options: Cold is conducted from the snow into the metal
The metal is a good conductor, so energy is transferred from the warmer metal to the snow
The metal reflects infrared onto the snow
The metal is a good emitter of convection
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Energy goes from the warmer metal into the colder snow by conduction. The direction matters: cold is not what moves.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: What happens to the amount of infrared radiation an object emits as its temperature rises?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: The hotter an object is, the more infrared radiation it emits.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: What is meant by thermal equilibrium?
options: The objects have the same mass
The objects are at the same temperature, so there is no net energy transfer
Energy transfer is at its fastest
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: When temperatures are equal there is no temperature difference, so no net energy transfer.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why does a cooling curve level off over time?
options: The object runs out of particles
The temperature difference gets smaller, so the rate of energy transfer decreases
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: The rate of transfer depends on the temperature difference. As the object approaches room temperature, the transfer slows.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why is air a poor conductor of thermal energy?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Gas particles are widely spaced, so they rarely pass energy on by collisions. That is why trapped air is used in insulation.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are at the same temperature. Why does the metal spoon feel colder to touch?
options: The metal is at a lower temperature
The metal conducts energy away from your hand faster
The metal absorbs cold from the air
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Both are at the same temperature. Metal is a good conductor, so energy leaves your hand faster and it feels colder.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why does a saucepan have a plastic handle?
options: Plastic is a poor conductor, so little energy reaches your hand
Plastic stops convection in the water
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Plastic is an insulator (poor conductor), so the handle stays cool.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: A lid is put on a cup of hot water. Which change does it cause?
options: Conduction through the sides stops completely
Less energy is lost from the surface by convection and evaporation, so it cools more slowly
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: A lid cuts losses from the top by convection and evaporation, so the water stays warmer for longer.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Which statement about conduction and convection is correct?
options: Both can happen in a vacuum
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Conduction needs particles to pass on vibrations; convection needs a fluid to flow. Only radiation needs no particles.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: A convection current is set up in a beaker of water heated at one side of the base. Where does the heated water go?
options: It rises above the heat, then moves across and sinks on the other side
It moves sideways along the bottom only
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Heated water is less dense and rises; it spreads across the top, cools and sinks on the far side, forming a circulating current.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Which is the correct explanation of why warm water is less dense than cold water?
options: The water particles move further apart, so the same mass takes up more volume
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Particles speed up and move further apart; the same mass fills a bigger volume, so density falls. Particles do not grow or lose mass.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: In a conduction practical, pins are fixed with wax to the ends of rods of different metals and the other ends are heated equally. How is the best conductor identified?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: The best conductor carries energy to the far end fastest, so its wax melts and its pin drops first.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: In the conduction practical in the previous question, which variable must be kept the same for a fair test?
options: The length and thickness of the rods
The time for each pin to fall
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Rods must be the same length and thickness so that only the material changes. The metal is the independent variable and the time is the dependent variable.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: A metal cube has one matt black face and one shiny silver face and is filled with hot water. Why must an infrared detector be held the same distance from each face?
options: So the detector does not melt
Because the reading also depends on distance, so only the surface should change
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: It is a control variable. Changing the distance would change the reading as well as the surface.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: A spinning satellite has a dull black bar and a shiny white bar. When the bars face away from the Sun, what happens?
options: The white bar cools faster because it is a better emitter
The black bar cools faster because it is a better emitter
Neither cools, because space is a vacuum
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Black is the better emitter, so it loses energy by radiation faster. There is no convection or conduction in space because there are no particles.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why is shiny foil sometimes placed on the wall behind a room heater?
options: To conduct energy into the wall
To reflect infrared back into the room
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: A shiny surface is a good reflector, so infrared that would warm the wall is sent back into the room.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: A room heater is often called a radiator. By which mechanism does it transfer most of its energy to the room?
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Air next to the heater warms, rises and is replaced by cooler air: most of the energy spreads round the room by convection.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: On a still day, a convection current in the air above snow slows its melting. Why?
options: Warm air rises away, leaving the coldest air next to the snow
Cold air rises away from the snow
The air reflects infrared onto the snow
Convection carries energy downwards into the snow
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Warmer air rises; the coldest, densest air stays nearest the snow, so the rate of energy transfer to the snow falls.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why does double glazing reduce energy loss through a window?
options: The glass is a good conductor
The gap between the panes contains air or a vacuum, which conducts poorly
It increases convection through the glass
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: The layer of air (or vacuum) between the panes reduces conduction, and a narrow gap limits convection.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Why does a wool jumper keep you warm?
options: Wool is a good emitter of infrared
Wool traps air, which reduces conduction and convection
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: The fibres trap air. Trapped air is a poor conductor and cannot form convection currents, so energy leaves your body slowly.

14-thermal-energy-transfer.q: Black paint on a car hardens faster than white paint under infrared lamps. Which explanation earns the marks?
options: Black absorbs more infrared, so more energy is transferred to it
14-thermal-energy-transfer.explain: Name the process and link it to colour: black is a better absorber of infrared, so it gains more energy in the same time. "Attracts heat" scores nothing.
